author: Peoria Standard
title: National discussion increases acceptance around grieving during holidays
text:
Paul Arco Media Relations Coordinato | OSF HealthCare, Featured Stories, IL
Paul Arco Media Relations Coordinato | OSF HealthCare, Featured Stories, IL
As grief becomes a more prominent topic in national media and podcasts, mental health professionals say that these conversations are making it easier for people to express their feelings of loss. Amy Brooke, MA, LCPC, a psychotherapist with OSF HealthCare, notes that programs like Anderson Cooper's podcast "All There Is" provide a public forum for discussing grief. She says the show normalizes mourning by sharing real experiences and demonstrating that happiness can exist alongside sorrow.
“I think it’s a great thing that they were talking about it, because a lot of times people who are grieving feel very alone and isolated and they’re afraid of doing it wrong, and so what the podcast does is it helps people see how things are similar and even how people grieve differently.” Brooke adds that the podcast highlights there is no single correct way to grieve, even though society often judges different approaches.
Brooke explains that each person's experience with grief is unique due to their individual relationship with the person who died. This means siblings within the same family may process loss in very different ways. She also stresses the importance of talking about loved ones as part of healing.
“A lot of times, when people are grieving, they sometimes feel like they’re bothering people if they talk about it, because ‘Oh, my mom died a year ago. I shouldn’t still be talking about her,’ but what the podcast does, it says, ‘No, it’s okay to talk about it if it’s 20 years ago.’”
Brooke advises those supporting someone in mourning to listen openly and allow them to share memories. “What it does is it makes it about transforming the loss rather than removing the person. We don’t want to remove the person from our lives. We’re grieving them because they were so important to us. Why would we want to get rid of them?”
She describes grief as neither linear nor cyclical but unpredictable—comparing its sudden emergence to “darts being thrown at your soul.” Recognizing these moments can help individuals understand unexpected emotions triggered by daily events or reminders.
Support groups offer another resource for those coping with loss. Brooke points out these groups provide connections that friends or family may not be able to give—especially for those worried about burdening others.
“It is very different than talking to your friends, because a lot of times with our friends, we’re afraid we’re burdening them, where, with a support group, you have time set aside to actually talk about that person, and even if you’re not talking about it, you’re listening to somebody else, and you’re giving that support to them, which can feel really good if you feel like you’ve just been taking.”
For those uncomfortable joining in-person groups, she suggests exploring online options tailored by type of loss.
Grief often intensifies during holidays when traditions highlight absence. Brooke encourages individuals experiencing loss during this time to adjust expectations and redefine what brings comfort during celebrations.
Her advice includes acknowledging changes in holiday routines and focusing on activities or traditions that bring personal comfort—even if they differ from past practices or others’ expectations.
“The energy we put into trying to make it the same is kind of harmful, because we’re using all of our energy to really try to do something that’s impossible.”
Despite increased public awareness around grief through media discussions and community guidance, Brooke observes persistent societal pressures—including limited bereavement leave at work—that push individuals toward moving on quickly after significant losses.
“We put a time limit on grief, and for example if someone’s mother dies we say you actually have three days off to deal with that grief and three days is not enough time to deal with a loss.”
She also notes society often overlooks losses beyond immediate family members—such as friends or neighbors—and encourages compartmentalization rather than processing feelings fully. Unaddressed grief can later manifest physically through fatigue or sleep issues as well as emotional symptoms such as anxiety or depression.
In some cases substance use may become an unhealthy coping mechanism when individuals suppress thoughts related to their loss. However mental health experts hope ongoing public dialogue will lead toward greater understanding for mourners whose needs do not fit standard timelines.
OSF HealthCare operates across Illinois and Michigan as an integrated nonprofit system providing hospitals,clinics, urgent-care centers,mental health care services,community guidance on well-being,and resources for patients facing various health challenges including emotional support after bereavement.
